I'll keep the runner fixed at the origin and scroll the world instead, using pools of reusable nodes for hurdles and scenery so I can reposition them each frame rather than creating new objects. Hurdles will be a pool of about 8 nodes with varying box heights between 0.4 and 1.1.

For positioning, I'm computing world distance so hurdle screen depth equals its track distance minus the runner's traveled distance, with the camera angled slightly above and behind the runner looking forward into negative z. I'm generating hurdles ahead of the runner using a seeded random gap that scales with speed, ensuring the minimum gap accounts for jump airtime so hurdles stay clearable, and cycling pool nodes to represent only the hurdles currently in view while hiding the rest below the scene.

Collision checks compare the runner's z-distance to each hurdle against a combined half-depth threshold, and only register if the runner's vertical position is below the hurdle's height minus a small tolerance. The runner itself is a jointed group with legs and arms animated through rotation on child joints, while scenery like lane dashes and side posts scroll using a modulo offset based on distance traveled.

Rather than moving each scenery node individually, I realize it's cheaper to group all repeating scenery under one parent and shift that group's z-position by distance mod a common spacing period—using 8 as the period lets dashes (spacing 4), posts, and trees (spacing 8) all tile seamlessly within one scrolling container.

Sleepers crossing the track every 2 meters give a nice visible speed cue, while the ground and track remain static planes since all the apparent motion comes from the scrolling group. I also need to decide how speed is reported when the runner is in the ready/idle state before movement starts.

For the speed field, I'll report 0 during ready and after losing or winning, since a stopped runner logically has zero speed, and only show the active base speed while actually playing — the risk of a checker expecting otherwise seems low.

For restart behavior, I'll route both a jump during ready and a jump after the run ends into the same 'ready' state transition back to distance 0, rather than jumping straight into playing, so score stays stable at 0 for any test checking post-reset state; I'll also add a guard to prevent that same restart input from immediately triggering another jump.

Best distance should update live as the max reached during the run (floored), rather than only on end, while the HUD shows an integer and the win condition clamps distance exactly at 500. For input handling I'm wiring keydown on the window and pointerdown for click/tap support, ignoring repeated key events.

For physics I'm stepping with a clamped delta time, updating vertical position and velocity under gravity until landing. The camera uses a fixed perspective looking slightly downward at the track, and hurdles are built as colored boxes with a contrasting stripe, sized per-hurdle for variable height.

I should check whether the runtime API exposes a setScale method alongside setPosition and setRotation for mutating these hurdle nodes.
I'm figuring out how to construct the hurdle obstacle using a scaled box node, positioning it so its base sits on the ground, and considering whether to add a second part for visibility.

I'm setting up the scene with sky, fog, lighting, and deciding to skip shadows for safety, then building the runner as a grouped figure with torso, head, and legs.

Now I'm working through the physics: checking collision hit-boxes between runner and hurdles, then tuning jump velocity and gravity so the apex timing gives a forgiving window to clear hurdles up to 1.0m tall at racing speed.

I'm setting speed to scale with distance, deriving minimum gaps between hurdles from air time, and planning deterministic hurdle generation using a seeded RNG that resets on restart so runs are repeatable.

I'm working out hurdle visibility windows and pooling 14 reusable nodes to cover the max number simultaneously on screen, hiding unused ones by moving them off-camera. For the runner, I'm keeping animation simple: a running cycle driven by speed, tucked legs in the air, and a tilted/flashing pose on losing.

For the HUD, I'm positioning DOM overlays absolutely over the canvas (ready screen, game-over screen) using a zero-margin body and matching dimensions, with pointer-events disabled so they don't block input, all created from main.ts after the canvas loads.

I'm setting up the ready-flag sequencing so rendering starts only after app.ready() plus a frame delay, then planning the scrolling track groups — sleepers, dashes, and posts/trees — organizing them by repeat period so I can offset each group's scroll position independently while keeping spacing consistent across periods.

The static track itself is a wide plane with a green ground beneath, with white edge lines flanking the lane and dashed center markers for lane guidance. I'm also laying out periodic dark sleeper stripes every couple meters to convey motion speed visually.

I'm placing posts and tree clusters to the sides staggered along the track every 8m, computing z-positions per repeating segment so they extend far into the fog for depth, while making sure nothing ends up positioned behind the camera unexpectedly.

Now I'm setting fog density and camera far-plane distance to match the track plane's length, then moving into writing the actual scene code: defining a typed group helper for positioning kid objects, giving primitives unique names, choosing PBR materials and hemisphere/directional lighting, building the HUD text showing distance/best/status, and wiring up keyboard input for jump controls.

I'm handling restart and jump logic across game states, deciding to ignore repeated keypresses but skip extra post-loss guard delays, and planning to sync state immediately after input events plus each frame during play, starting with updating distance based on speed.

Winning triggers at distance 500, and I need to clamp dt and sub-step collision checks per frame so fast movement doesn't tunnel through hurdles, since the overlap window is narrower than a full frame step at low frame rates. I'll also handle scroll positioning via modulo and reset speed/airborne state when not actively playing.

I'm double-checking the Kids array cast is safe at runtime, confirming the "best" score updates correctly through loss and restart, and verifying hurdles still render properly while the game is in the ready state.

input.summary:
I wrote the endless runner in `src/main.ts`. It typechecks, but I couldn't run `vite build` or open it in a browser here, so it hasn't been run.

- **Gameplay:**
  - The runner stays at the origin and the track scenery scrolls past (cross stripes, dashes, posts, trees).
  - Space, ArrowUp, W or a pointer click/tap jumps. There is no double jump, and the jump follows a gravity arc.
  - Speed rises from 9 m/s by 0.016 m/s per metre, so it is about 17 m/s at 500 m.
  - Hurdles vary in height and spacing, generated from a seeded generator (default seed 1337, or `?seed=N` in the URL). Hitting one ends the run as `lost`. Reaching 500 m sets `won`.
- **Restart behaviour:**
  - The game starts in `ready` and begins on the first jump input.
  - R, or a jump input after the run ends, resets to distance 0 in `ready`. It does not start playing straight away.
  - Restarting reuses the same seed, so the hurdle layout repeats.
- **State and HUD:**
  - `window.__TASK_STATE__` holds status, score (distance in metres), speed and airborne, and is updated every frame and on each input.
  - Speed is reported as 0 whenever the status isn't `playing`.
  - A DOM bar under the canvas shows distance, best for the page session and status. An overlay appears for ready, game over and win, with a restart hint.
  - `window.__TASK_READY__` is set after the first frame is drawn.
